title: GNP and the per-person measure

blocks.heading: GNP and the per-person measure
blocks.text: GNP is the value of final output attributable to a country's residents over a period, including net income from abroad. Distinguish the national total from a per-person figure. GNP per person is GNP divided by the population; an average that does not show how income is distributed. Use the same period and compatible currency units in a comparison. A larger population can produce a larger total without having more resources per person.

blocks.heading: Show the division and the unit
blocks.text: For a fictional country, annual GNP is N$240 million and population is 12,000. GNP per person = N$240,000,000 ÷ 12,000 = N$20,000 per person per year. Write out the millions before dividing, or keep a consistent power-of-ten method. This answer is an average, not the wage of a typical worker. If another fictional country has GNP of N$300 million and 30,000 residents, its average is N$10,000 per person per year despite its larger total.

blocks.heading: Use it for an appropriate judgement
blocks.text: For fictional Area H, average annual income per person is N$50,000 and safe-water access 40%; J has N$30,000 and 85%. An income-only rule prioritises J. For improving water access, H’s larger access gap provides stronger evidence of need. Income and access answer different questions: compare the measure directly relevant to the decision.

blocks.heading: Why an income average is incomplete
blocks.text: GNP per person divides a national aggregate by population, so unequal distribution can leave many households with low incomes despite a high average. Unrecorded household farming and informal sales can make measured output incomplete. Money income does not show whether people can obtain safe water, education or health care. It also leaves out losses such as damaged habitats and the value of unpaid care. Price differences change what a given income buys, so international comparisons need a comparable basis. An average may help compare economic resources, but combine it with evidence on distribution, services and environmental conditions before judging living standards.
